questions.prompt: A fund has cumulative distributions of 160 and paid-in capital of 150. What is its DPI?
questions.explanation: DPI = D / PIC = 160 / 150 = 1.0667x. Rounded to three decimal places: 1.067x.

questions.prompt: Using the same fund (PIC = 150, distributions = 160, NAV = 40), what is the RVPI?
Using the same fund (PIC = 150, distributions = 160, NAV = 40), what is the TVPI?
Verify TVPI = DPI + RVPI for the example fund (PIC = 150, D = 160, NAV = 40). What is DPI + RVPI (to three decimal places)?
questions.explanation: DPI = 1.067x, RVPI = 0.267x. DPI + RVPI = 1.333x = TVPI = 200/150. The identity holds exactly by construction.

questions.prompt: A deal invests 100 at t=0 and exits at 200 at t=4 (no sub line). What is the IRR? Use the formula (2)^(1/4) − 1 and express as a percentage rounded to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: IRR = 2^(1/4) − 1 = 1.18921 − 1 = 0.18921 = 18.92%. This is the base-case IRR with a 2.0x multiple over 4 years.

questions.prompt: The same deal (invest 100, exit at 200) uses a sub line so LP capital is called 1 year later (t=1) and the exit is still at t=4 with no interest cost. What is the new IRR? Use (2)^(1/3) − 1, expressed as a percentage rounded to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Now money is at risk for only 3 years: IRR = 2^(1/3) − 1 = 1.25992 − 1 = 0.25992 = 25.99%. Compared to 18.92% base case — ~7 points of IRR purely from timing, with zero additional value.

questions.prompt: Using the full worked fund (calls 100 @ yr 0, 50 @ yr 1; distributions 60 @ yr 3, 100 @ yr 5; terminal NAV 40 @ yr 5; index 100→110→130→150), what is the KS-PME (to three decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Compound all flows to t=5 using I_T/I_t factors. Numerator (distributions + NAV): 60×(150/130) + 100×1 + 40×1 = 69.23 + 100 + 40 = 209.23. Denominator (contributions): 100×(150/100) + 50×(150/110) = 150 + 68.18 = 218.18. KS-PME = 209.23 / 218.18 = 0.959.

questions.prompt: For the same fund and index, what is the Direct Alpha (annualized excess return over the index), to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: Scale each CF by I_T/I_t: −100×1.5=−150 @ t0; −50×1.3636=−68.18 @ t1; +60×1.1538=+69.23 @ t3; +140×1.0=+140 @ t5. IRR of this index-adjusted stream = −1.03%/yr. Negative = underperformance.

questions.prompt: In the NAV-loan example (PIC = 100, prior distributions = 20, NAV = 100), after a 30 NAV loan is distributed to LPs, what is the new DPI?
questions.explanation: New cumulative distributions = 20 + 30 = 50. DPI = 50 / 100 = 0.50x. No value was created; the cash came from debt. TVPI remains 1.20x pre-interest (the distributed cash is offset by new fund-level debt reducing net NAV from 100 to 70).

questions.prompt: KS-PME = 1.20 means which of the following?
choices: The fund's IRR was 20% per year
The fund returned 20% more total wealth to the LP than an identically-timed index investment
The fund outperformed the index by 20 basis points per year
questions.explanation: KS-PME is a wealth ratio. 1.20 means the LP ended with 20% more terminal wealth than if they had put the same cash flows, on the same dates, into the index. It is not annualized, so it cannot be read as a per-year rate.

questions.prompt: A GP reports a 30% net IRR alongside only a 1.4x TVPI. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Exceptional deal selection with very fast value creation
Subscription-line usage inflating IRR without expanding the multiple
The fund is still in its J-curve with most NAV unrealized
The fund's management fee is unusually low
questions.explanation: A high IRR combined with a modest multiple is the fingerprint of subscription-line usage or very fast capital return (quick flips/dividend recaps). The sub line shortens LP capital duration, mechanically lifting IRR while leaving TVPI ~flat (or slightly lower due to interest costs).

questions.prompt: Why does a NAV-loan-funded distribution NOT improve TVPI (before interest)?
choices: Because the cash paid out is exactly offset by new fund-level debt that reduces net NAV by the same amount
Because TVPI only counts realized cash, not paper NAV
Because NAV loans are secured by uncalled commitments
questions.explanation: The loan proceeds are distributed (increasing D), but the fund now carries new debt that reduces net NAV by the same amount. (D + NAV) stays the same before interest, so TVPI = (D + NAV) / PIC is unchanged. After interest, TVPI falls.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the 'shortness problem' of Long–Nickels PME?
choices: The synthetic index portfolio can underestimate returns on short-duration funds
Large distributions by a strong outperformer imply selling more index than the synthetic portfolio holds, making synthetic NAV negative and the PME IRR incalculable
The method cannot handle funds with fewer than 5 cash flows
LN-PME overstates performance when the index is declining
questions.explanation: On strong outperformers, distributions are large and LN sells those dollar amounts of the index. If cumulative sells exceed the synthetic portfolio's value, the synthetic NAV goes negative — i.e., the method is effectively short the index. The PME IRR becomes incalculable or nonsensical. mPME and PME+ were invented to fix this.

questions.prompt: A fund has been running for 10 years. Its TVPI is 2.4x, but DPI is only 0.3x and RVPI is 2.1x. Write a 3–4 sentence analyst assessment, covering what the numbers mean, what risks they imply, and what you would do next.
questions.modelAnswer: This fund's 2.4x TVPI is almost entirely unrealized: 2.1x (87.5%) is still sitting as the GP's marks (RVPI), while only 0.3x has been returned as actual cash (DPI). Ten years in, a healthy buyout fund should have realized substantially more, so this DPI level raises questions about exit pace and mark quality. The key risk is that the paper 2.4x does not materialize — NAVs could be aggressively marked, exits slow in current markets, or a continuation-fund or NAV-loan structure may be deferring realizations. Next steps: scrutinize the valuation methodology for each portfolio company (third-party validation, recent transactions for comps), check whether any distributions came from NAV-loan proceeds rather than genuine exits, look at whether a continuation fund is being used to roll hard-to-exit assets, and compute the PME to assess whether the unrealized marks look supportable relative to the public market. Weight DPI and PME heavily in any assessment; TVPI here is the GP's opinion, not a track record.
